title: WNBA Finals Game 6: Why is it being played at 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday? - CBS Sports
description: It took a lot of moving parts for a potential championship-deciding game to be played on a weekday afternoon
body:
It took a lot of moving parts for a potential championship-deciding game to be played on a weekday afternoon
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 29, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:00 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Game 6 of the 2026 WNBA Finals between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream will tip off at 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday at State Farm Arena. The lunch time start for the first Game 6 in WNBA history -- the Finals were expanded to a best-of-seven last season -- has drawn plenty of confusion and criticism. Before the Valkyries, up 3-2 in the series, attempt to win the first title in franchise history, and the Dream try to keep their season alive, here's everything you need to know about one of the most unique title-deciding games in recent sports history. State Farm Arena not yet Dream's primary homeEarlier this month, the Dream announced a multi-year deal to play all of their games at State Farm Arena, also the home of the NBA's Atlanta Hawks, starting with the 2027 season, in an effort to meet the "unprecedented growth of the franchise, increasing ticket demand and overall excitement for the entire Dream fan experience."But for this season, the Dream's primary home was still Gateway Center Arena, which is where they've played since 2021. Gateway Center Arena holds just 3,500 people and is the smallest arena in the WNBA. 
The Dream were able to move five regular-season games to State Farm Arena, which holds 17,000 people, as well as their first five postseason games, but it's important to establish that they are not yet the primary tenants in the arena, which is why there have been so many scheduling conflicts.  
        
            
                Dream owners decry midday Finals Game 6 after scheduling chaos: 'Earned the right to be taken seriously'
                
                    Jack Maloney                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Dream, Hawks have different ownersAnother key fact to establish is that, unlike many WNBA and NBA teams that play in the same city, the Dream and the Hawks -- the primary tenant of State Farm Arena -- have different owners. The Dream are owned by Larry and Robyn Gottesdiener, Suzanne Abair and former Dream player Renee Montgomery. The Hawks are owned by a group led by Tony Ressler. The franchises have collaborated, but the different ownership groups are another reason for the logistical challenges that have arisen during this playoff run. 
Previous Finals games had to be adjustedThe Dream had no trouble moving their first round and semifinal games to State Farm Arena, but now that the NBA's regular season is underway, the building has much less flexibility. Games 3 and 4 of the Finals, the first two the Dream hosted, had to be rescheduled to take place at State Farm Arena. Game 3 was moved from Oct. 22 to Oct. 21, while Game 4 was moved up to 1 p.m. ET in order to accommodate a doubleheader with the Hawks' matchup against the Houston Rockets, which was moved back to 8 p.m. 
        
            
                WNBA Finals' Game 6 scheduling debacle is an embarrassing end to a historic season
                
                    Lindsay Gibbs                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
No good options for Game 6Moving Games 3 and 4 took some collaboration with the Hawks, the NBA and broadcast partners, but was ultimately not that complicated. Instead of having two days off in Atlanta between Games 2 and 3, they moved Game 3 up to an open date and had two days off between Games 3 and 4. And, because Game 4 was set for a Saturday, a Dream-Hawks doubleheader was more than doable. 
However, there were no good options for Game 6. The Hawks play at home on Wednesday and Thursday and are off on Friday before playing again on Saturday. Game 7, meanwhile, is set for Saturday in San Francisco, if necessary. The WNBA couldn't move Game 6 to Wednesday because the Hawks have a home game against the Miami Heat.Because of Wednesday's game, the Hawks could not move Thursday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers to the afternoon because the NBA's CBA requires teams to have at least 22 hours before games.Moving Thursday's Hawks-Cavaliers game to Friday was technically possible, as both teams are off that night, but it would have created major logistical issues for both teams and broadcast partners. In addition, Friday nights are supposed to be NBA Cup exclusive nights, and the Hawks-Cavaliers game is not a Cup matchup.That ultimately left the WNBA with three realistic options, all of which had major downsides:Play Game 6 on Thursday night at Gateway Center Arena;Play Game 6 on Thursday afternoon at State Farm Arena; orDrastically alter the Finals schedule and move Game 6 to Friday at State Farm Arena, and Game 7, if necessary, to Nov. 3 at Chase Center.Ultimately, the league chose to take the Thursday afternoon route in order to ensure the game was played at State Farm Arena without making major changes to the overall Finals schedule. 
"The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere at State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success, and we're excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line," WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said in a press release announcing the decision. "We thank the NBA, Dream, Valkyries, Hawks, State Farm Arena and USA Network for the collaboration and flexibility that made this move possible. We look forward to delivering another unforgettable Finals experience in Atlanta."Dream, WNBA at odds over final decisionThe Dream's ownership group released an open letter to the city of Atlanta and Dream fans on Tuesday. In the letter, the ownership group claimed that it raised concerns months ago about potential scheduling conflicts at State Farm Arena that "did not receive the attention, nor the urgency that they deserved." Additionally, the letter noted that "playing a midday game on a Thursday is not what we would have chosen and not what we fought for."
However, according to a memo obtained by The Athletic, the WNBA had sent out "playoff hold dates" to teams back on Dec. 4, 2025, and all 15 teams had until Dec. 31 to respond with potential arena conflicts. If there was a potential issue, teams were told to explain the "nature of the conflict." As previously noted, however, State Farm Arena is not the Dream's primary home. It's unclear how the process for holding playoff dates at an alternate arena works. A Dream spokesperson declined comment on the matter to The Athletic. Game 6 sells out anywayThere were, and still are, understandable concerns about what the crowd and viewership numbers might look like for a Finals game played in the middle of a workday, but the Dream announced Wednesday that Game 6 is a sellout. 
"Perhaps it was assumed that the Dream would not make it this far. Perhaps, our place in the Finals was not accounted for," the Dream's ownership group wrote in their letter. "Whatever the reason, the reality is that we are here. We earned our place in the Finals, and our city deserves the opportunity to show up for its team."

title: Sergio Garcia announces return to DP World Tour in 2027, eyes Ryder Cup, PGA Tour - CBS Sports
description: The Spaniard still has high hopes as he approaches the half century mark
body:
The Spaniard still has high hopes as he approaches the half century mark
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 29, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:40 am ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Sergio Garcia announced Thursday his plans to return to the DP World Tour in 2027. The Masters champion had called LIV Golf home since the league's first event in London in June 2022, but made it clear through the bankruptcy proceedings that he did not see a future with LIV Golf 2.0.Garcia also made it known that he hopes to return to the PGA Tour down the road. The 46-year-old's last appearance on the PGA Tour came in May 2022 at the Wells Fargo Championship at TPC Potomac where he expressed his disdain for the league while looking for a lost ball."Next season I'll be playing on the DP World Tour," Garcia released in a statement. "This tour has been a huge part of my career from the very beginning, and I'm proud to call it home again. I'm also keeping my options open for a return to the PGA Tour. And probably the most exciting part for me is strengthening personal relationships, both new and old."There are some great tournaments around the world to play before Augusta next April, and I can't wait to get back to the Masters. I left Augusta last year disappointed with myself and my actions, and I'm ready to show what I've learned and where I am mentally. Augusta has given me some of the greatest moments of my life, and I'd love nothing more than to chase another green jacket at such a special place. I'm excited to get to work and excited to grind."
Even as he approaches 50, Garcia remains motivated by playing a role on the European Ryder Cup team. At the Open de España in early October, the 15-time DP World Tour winner revealed that he had discussed with European Ryder Cup captain Luke Donald about contributing in some capacity in 2027.
As it stands, however, the DP World Tour has a rule in place barring any golfer who dropped membership for any reason to be a captain or vice captain for the European Ryder Cup team. In May 2023, Garcia resigned his DP World Tour membership along with fellow Ryder Cup stalwarts Ian Poulter and Lee Westwood meaning he would have to play his way onto the team to be there in Ireland next year."It's a big year ahead with the Ryder Cup, and I'm going to work my tail off for every chance I can get at more majors and the biggest events in the game," Garcia said. "Another goal is to make that Ryder Cup team, and to be an asset to the guys in whatever capacity that may be. In golf, everything is earned and nothing is given. Let's get to work."The DP World Tour took a firm stance ahead of the 2027 season regarding players' abilities to double dip in the form of playing on both the European circuit and LIV Golf. The league made it so that those players who choose to participate in LIV Golf 2.0 are unable to take up membership on the DP World Tour, effectively blocking them out of the Ryder Cup as all members of the European team must be members of the DP World Tour.
Garcia remains the all-time points leader in Ryder Cup history even with his absence the last two iterations. He boasts an impressive 28.5 points across 10 appearances for the European side with his last showing coming in 2021 at Whistling Straits.

title: Clemson's offensive collapse under Dabo Swinney has Tigers facing harsh reality - CBS Sports
description: Once an explosive unit that developed future NFL stars at QB, Clemson has devolved into one of the worst offenses
body:
Once an explosive unit that developed future NFL stars at QB, Clemson has devolved into one of the worst offenses in college football
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 29, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:45 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        In Clemson's slow descent from championship program to ACC also-ran, the starkest decline has appeared on offense. The frustration is growing, and Dabo Swinney was seen on camera on the sideline last Saturday against Virginia Tech with a large playsheet in hand, which he says is not a rarity, but it did nothing to help rumors of discontent with offensive coordinator Chad Morris and questions about whether Swinney himself took the wheel during the game. Morris was offensive coordinator for the Tigers for four seasons from 2011-2014 as Clemson began its ascent. He was brought in to arrest the slide, and he clearly isn't. They were Nick Saban's greatest foil at Alabama, and now they struggle to even score 30 points.A month ago, CBS Sports reported that firing Swinney was unlikely due to finances, so an increasingly unhappy marriage may continue. But for now, for this season, just how bad it is on offense punctuates how far Clemson has fallen.
From QB factory to offensive futilityAt first under Dabo Swinney, Clemson was at the forefront of the spread era.It was fun, fresh and uptempo, with plenty of points. They became a wide receiver factory (Swinney is a wide receivers coach by trade) and, most importantly, an incubator of quarterback talent. Few programs ever have a quarterback as good as Deshaun Watson or Trevor Lawrence. Clemson had them both within only one year of each other. Now they sit as one of the nation's worst passing offenses, and near the bottom third of most offensive stats overall. Since former offensive coordinator Tony Elliott left in 2021, Clemson has struggled for a true offensive identity.  Brandon Streeter was an internal promotion who lasted a year in 2022. Garrett Riley represented Swinney as acquiescing to the demand for an outside voice, which never really worked; now Swinney is back to Morris. Saturday's Virginia Tech game saw the Tigers score one offensive touchdown, and a frustrated Swinney minced no words after the first two quarters. 
"It's all coaching," Dabo Swinney told ESPN going into halftime after his offense scored three points in the first half against Virginia Tech. "That's 100% coaching. Pitiful. Pitiful. 100% coaching. That ain't the players, that's us.""I just don't think we helped them enough to win the game with some decisions and play calls," Swinney said after the game. "Those kids played their butts off."Swinney told reporters Sunday night he will stick with Morris as offensive coordinator the rest of the season. The offense that they are all overseeing has been putrid. 
Clemson is last in percentage of points from offensive touchdowns. They're 133rd in touchdowns scored (14) and 112th in scoring offense (21.4). Clemson ranks 138th out of 138 teams in passing touchdowns this season and has not thrown one in four games. Their only two passing TDs came against Georgia Southern and North Carolina. The Tigers are also 115th nationally in passing yards per game. They have more interceptions (seven) than TDs and have gone 164 dropbacks without a touchdown, according to TruMedia.  Tait Reynolds is last among Power Four quarterbacks in QBR. The Tigers are tied for 103rd in total plays of 20+ yards, and 106th in passing plays going 20+ yards (17). According to CBS Sports research, Clemson has scored 28 points or fewer in 10 straight games against FBS teams, the longest such streak since 2008 (coincidentally, broken in Dabo's first home win as Clemson head coach). The only longer streaks in school history are 15 games (1993-1995) and 11 (1979-1980).
No easy fix in sightIt is hard to see how Clemson's offense gets significantly better. Swinney even benched his only somewhat prolific offensive player, Gideon Davidson, due to poor play in the Virginia Tech game. 
The Tigers had found some success running the ball in late September, but it all makes for a truly laborious watch. The advanced stats are similarly unkind. Clemson has been to the red zone 23 times in seven games (T-103 nationally) and is 104th nationally in red zone scores. Their drives gain only 37.9% of available yards (126th nationally), according to college football data analyst Brian Fremeau. Clemson is 126th in success rate (37.6), 104th in three-and-out percentage (30.2), 136th in EPA per play (-.10), 130th in yards per play (4.85) and 109th in plays for zero or negative yards (33.1%). Clemson was never an offensive line factory, even when they were at the peak of the sport, and has allowed 21 sacks (123rd nationally) and has a sack rate of 8% (123rd nationally) this season. 
Swinney told reporters that the quarterback battle would have been ongoing between Reynolds and Christopher Vizzina had Vizzina not gotten hurt early in the year. Swinney left the door open to the possibility of seeing more Vizzina later in the season, but affirmed that Reynolds is still the starter. There is no telling how far Clemson can slide. Their five remaining games, including Saturday vs. Florida State, are all toss-ups, and even that is its own treatise on where Clemson is, given Syracuse, Duke, and Georgia Tech remain -- ACC teams that Clemson would have never dreamed of sharing a cul-de-sac with even three years ago. But that's the program Clemson is right now under Swinney.

title: Ohio State, Georgia among top-25 teams on upset alert in Week 9 - CBS Sports
description: These five college football games on Saturday offer plenty of upset potential
body:
These five college football games on Saturday offer plenty of upset potential
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 29, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:00 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        No team is immune to college football's upset bug this season.Georgia caught the sickness earlier this month in the form of Auburn's walk-off win inside Sanford Stadium, squandering the Bulldogs' brief stay at No. 1. While they've had symptoms in the form of close calls, the FBS' remaining unbeatens -- Miami, Utah and UCLA -- just haven't experienced the bite yet.That could happen Saturday for the Utes, who travel to Cincinnati coming off the Bearcats' takedown of Texas Tech during the Big 12's multi-team CFP path hiccup last weekend. Utah's one of five teams on upset alert in Week 9 inside the top 25 ahead of Tuesday night's first College Football Playoff rankings reveal.Those initial opinions from the selection committee will provide some detail on the conference valuations, record strength, and the impact of quality wins this fall. Several more could come this weekend.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 2 Ohio StateOpponent: at USC (+6.5)Ryan Day declined to name his starting quarterback for Saturday's bout with the Trojans, but the assumption is that true freshman Luke Fahey is getting the nod after relieving Julian Sayin two weeks ago against Indiana. How much does this offense change with a newcomer back there? Will the game plan be neutered a bit against a quality opponent on the road? These are questions we don't have answers to yet, which is why this is a prime upset spot for the Big Ten's current co-leader with UCLA.
"We all got to be tighter here. We got to help a young quarterback get his first win as a Buckeye. And it's going to take our best," Day said Monday. "And that means everyone that's part of the program has got to be really good in everything that we do. So extra focus this week. Not that we need to be focused any more; I mean, obviously, we know how good of a team USC is, and we know the talent, we know the coaches, we know everything about it. And we know what we're up against this week. But having a new starting quarterback is just another reason to stay even more focused."
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 3 Georgia Opponent: vs. Florida (+11.5)Both teams had an extra week to prep for the rivalry showdown at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, but Florida's Jon Sumrall has kept his plan at quarterback coy from the Bulldogs. Tramell Jones Jr. starred in place of injured starter Aaron Philo at Texas last time out and was terrific, giving Buster Faulkner and Florida's offensive staff quite the dilemma ahead of their biggest game to date. Georgia now has film on both players, but the offensive tweaks change a bit depending on who trots out there with the first team. 
        
            
                Year 1 vs. Year 11: Jon Sumrall's Florida rebuild faces ultimate measuring stick -- Georgia
                
                    Brandon Marcello                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Independent of Florida's offensive changes, Georgia simply needs to focus on not beating itself in Week 9. The Bulldogs rank fourth-best in the SEC at plus-3 this season in turnover margin, but failed to deliver against Auburn following Gunner Stockton's three giveaways. If turnovers are an issue again, Florida could win this one despite being a double-digit underdog.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 6 UtahOpponent: at Cincinnati (+6.5)Coming off the emotional high of last week's win over then-unbeaten Texas Tech, doing it all over again vs. the Utes is top priority for Scott Satterfield and the Bearcats this weekend. Utah offers a considerably more difficult challenge, boasting one of the nation's top run defenses while also flexing the Big 12's second-best scoring offense (37.4 points per game) and the Big 12's second-best total offense at 478.4 ypg. One of three unbeatens left in the Power Four, Utah must contain junior running back Cole Tabb, who rushed for a season-high 173 yards and a score last time out and is averaging 9.6 yards per carry to lead the Big 12. There's the lookahead angle, too. The Utes host BYU in a mammoth showdown with CFP implications on Nov. 7, but the Holy War loses some of its luster if Utah goes to Cincinnati and falters.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 13 Texas TechOpponent: vs. No. 22 Arizona (+3.5)We'll see if the Red Raiders have anything left in the tank as a narrow home favorite against the streaking Wildcats, who have won five straight since an early-season loss at BYU. Texas Tech gave up four touchdown passes during its loss at Cincinnati, and Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita has the talent -- 2,064 yards passing, 18 touchdowns this season -- to torch this secondary again if coverage breakdowns remain an issue. Joey McGuire's 8-8 in his career against top-25 opponents, which is the best winning percentage (.500) in the Big 12. A win this weekend keeps all season-long goals still within reach for his team.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 23 MissouriOpponent: at Arkansas (+9.5)After ending its SEC losing skid at Vanderbilt on Oct. 17, the Razorbacks hope to perform in a rivalry spot against a ranked foe still clinging to CFP hopes as one of several two-loss SEC squads. Arkansas first-year coach Ryan Silverfield said this week "it's good to have some hate" in prep for the Tigers, but acknowledged he's treating this one like any other game in Week 9 at home. We know it's not for a program that's 2-10 in this series since Missouri entered the SEC in 2014. Tigers running back Ahmad Hardy returned to practice this week for the first time this season after recovering from a gunshot wound suffered in May while attending a concert. His availability for Saturday is TBD, per Eli Drinkwitz.

        Kentucky's rise to No. 1 in college football's Week 9 resume rankings illustrates why the totality of what a team has done should be evaluated in debates over postseason credentials.While it's technically true that -- based on the AP poll -- a win over LSU is UK's only "ranked" win entering Week 9, it's worth peeling back the layers a bit. Doing so reveals that Kentucky has some fortification on its ledger. The Wildcats own road wins over Texas A&M, South Carolina and Oklahoma. All three are power-rated as top-30 teams in Andrew Percival's CFB Metrics Consensus.The CFB Metrics Consensus folds 10 different power ratings into a single metric to paint a true picture of how difficult an opponent is to beat. It is the new baseline metric for our weekly resume rankings, which give Kentucky a significant edge on No. 2 UCLA. Using a consensus rating as the baseline helps eliminate any perceived biases that may be present in any single rating.Using a consensus power rating as the baseline for evaluating resumes helps the SEC. For example, a two-loss Texas team lands at No. 5 this week. Though the Ole Miss team Texas just beat is now No. 12 in the AP poll, the Rebels are No. 9 in the CFB Metrics Consensus. The Longhorns also own wins over No. 1 Ohio State and a road win over No. 11 Texas.
The resume rankings use a simple formula inspired by the NCAA's Wins Above Bubble (WAB) metric in college basketball. For our purposes, it measures the likelihood that the average No. 25 team in the CFB Metrics Consensus would win a game. No. 25 would beat No. 26 on a neutral field roughly 51% of the time. Thus, a neutral-site win over No. 26 will yield a 0.49 addition to a team's resume score.If you beat a top-five team on the road? Hey-O! That's a gold mine. Auburn added 0.91 to its resume score based on its win at No. 4 Georgia, reflecting that the average No. 25 team would only win that game 9% of the time. Road wins are more valuable than home wins.

title: NFL Draft's first-round gamble: What teams can learn from Super Bowl winners and failed rebuilds - CBS Sports
description: Three of the NFL's most recent Super Bowl champions have something in common. The Chiefs used two first-round picks in 2022 on Trent McD
body:
Three of the NFL's most recent Super Bowl champions have something in common. The Chiefs used two first-round picks in 2022 on Trent McDuffie and George Karlaftis, then won back-to-back championships. The Eagles took Jalen Carter and Nolan Smith in 2023 and won the Super Bowl two seasons later. And the Seahawks also drafted Devon Witherspoon and Jaxon Smith-Njigba in 2023, with both developing into stars before Seattle won it all in February.But there's another side to this story, and the New York Jets know it all too well. They had three first-round selections in 2022, landed some pretty good players, and somehow never made the playoffs. Four seasons later, only one of those players remains on the roster.The Cleveland Browns have been down this road, too. They made five first-round picks across the 2017 and 2018 drafts, eventually won a playoff game, but couldn't sustain that success. And now the Tennessee Titans are joining the party. With a 1-6 record, the No. 2 overall pick in 2027 as we sit here and two additional first-round selections coming from Chicago in exchange for Jeffery Simmons, Tennessee has gone all-in on accumulating draft capital. The Jets and Browns have plenty of picks of their own.So what separates the teams that turn extra first-round picks into championships from those that find themselves starting over? Having Patrick Mahomes certainly helps, but not every Super Bowl winner needs a first-ballot Hall of Famer under center. Put differently: How much comes down to making the right picks, and how much depends on everything else?
To answer that, we went back through every NFL Draft since 2000 and found 103 instances in which a team had multiple first-round picks. In all, those teams selected 216 players, including 25 quarterbacks. And as we've seen play out in real time, there's a big difference between finding good players and building a winning football team.2022 Jets: Three first-rounders, zero playoff appearancesIt's easy to forget how promising the Jets' 2022 draft looked. They took Sauce Gardner fourth overall, Garrett Wilson at No. 10 and then traded back into Round 1 for Jermaine Johnson at No. 26. Gardner and Wilson were named Defensive and Offensive Rookie of the Year, while Johnson became a Pro Bowler in his second season.Three first-round selections, two Rookie of the Year winners and a Pro Bowl pass rusher. You can't really draw it up any better than that.
The individual success, however, didn't translate to wins. The Jets went 7-10 in 2022 and 2023, then 5-12 and 3-14 the following two seasons. They cycled through quarterbacks, fired head coach Robert Saleh during the 2024 season and eventually moved on from general manager Joe Douglas, too. Then came the roster reset. Gardner was traded to Indianapolis in November 2025 for two first-round picks and receiver Adonai Mitchell. Johnson, who suffered a torn Achilles in 2024, was dealt to Tennessee for defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat in March 2026. Only Wilson remains.From a scouting standpoint, it's hard to call the 2022 draft a failure. But from a team-building standpoint? Four losing seasons, no playoffs, a fired coach and GM, and two of those three first-rounders playing elsewhere tell a different story.The Jets, you might remember, weren't the only New York team with multiple first-rounders that year.
2022 Giants: Two top-seven selections, one massive missThe Giants selected Kayvon Thibodeaux fifth overall and Evan Neal two picks later, hoping they had found an edge rusher and a franchise offensive tackle. Outside of quarterback, those are the two most valuable positions on the field, and to solve them early in the first round certainly made sense.New York made the playoffs in 2022 and even won a playoff game. But after that 9-7-1 season, the Giants won just six, three and four games over the following three years. Thibodeaux, while he hasn't lived up to lofty expectations, has shown he can get after the quarterback, including an 11.5-sack season in 2023. Neal, meanwhile, struggled with injuries and inconsistent play at right tackle, prompting the Giants to move him to guard in 2025. He didn't play a snap that season because of a hamstring injury, was released before the 2026 season and is now on the Raiders' practice squad. The Jets' problem wasn't necessarily identifying talented players. The Giants' problem was that one of their two premium selections failed to deliver. Different circumstances, same disappointing result.
And recent history offers plenty of contrasting examples.Recent teams with multiple first-round picks: What happened next?DraftTeamFirst-round selectionsWins by season after draftPlayoff appearances2022ChiefsTrent McDuffie, George Karlaftis14, 11, 15, 63; 2 Super Bowl titles2022LionsAidan Hutchinson, Jameson Williams9, 12, 15, 922022JetsSauce Gardner, Garrett Wilson, Jermaine Johnson7, 7, 5, 302022GiantsKayvon Thibodeaux, Evan Neal9, 6, 3, 412022RavensKyle Hamilton, Tyler Linderbaum10, 13, 12, 832023TexansC.J. Stroud, Will Anderson Jr.10, 10, 1232023LionsJahmyr Gibbs, Jack Campbell12, 15, 922023EaglesJalen Carter, Nolan Smith11, 14, 113; Super Bowl title2023SeahawksDevon Witherspoon, Jaxon Smith-Njigba9, 10, 141; Super Bowl title2024BearsCaleb Williams, Rome Odunze5, 1112024VikingsJ.J. McCarthy, Dallas Turner14, 912024CardinalsMarvin Harrison Jr., Darius Robinson8, 30The Lions and Texans: How to rebuild with extra picksDetroit and Houston were in very different situations when they entered their respective drafts, but both offer examples of how quickly things can change when a franchise gets it right.The Lions were coming off a 3-13-1 season when they selected Aidan Hutchinson second overall in 2022, then traded up to No. 12 for Jameson Williams. Detroit improved to 9-8 that fall, and a year later, the Lions were back in the first round with two more selections, taking running back Jahmyr Gibbs at No. 12 and linebacker Jack Campbell at No. 18.Four first-rounders in two drafts, and the results soon followed. Detroit went 12-5 in 2023 and reached the NFC Championship Game, then won 15 games the following season. Hutchinson became one of the NFL's best pass rushers, Gibbs emerged as one of the NFL's best backs, and Williams and Campbell developed into important contributors.What made Detroit's turnaround different was that it didn't need to find a quarterback. Jared Goff arrived in the 2021 Matthew Stafford trade, seemingly a throw-in alongside the two first-rounders the Lions received from the Rams. But GM Brad Holmes knew Goff from their time together in LA, and while the Rams were ready to move on, Holmes believed he could still be a franchise quarterback. So instead of drafting his replacement, the Lions built around him.Houston, meanwhile, needed a quarterback. Coming off a 3-13-1 season, the Texans selected CJ Stroud second overall in 2023, then traded up one spot later for Will Anderson Jr., and it wasn't cheap. Houston sent Arizona picks 12 and 33 that year, plus first- and third-rounders in 2024. But Anderson has been so good that no one even thinks to bring up what the Texans gave up to get him.The payoff was immediate: Houston went 10-7 in each of the next two seasons, then 12-5 in 2025, making the playoffs all three years. Stroud and Anderson became foundational pieces, even if Stroud couldn't quite match his brilliant rookie season in '24 and '25. And hiring DeMeco Ryans before that draft was just as important. The Texans found their quarterback, improved their pass rush and put a coaching staff in place that could develop the rest of the roster.The Chiefs, Eagles and Seahawks: How good teams stayed goodThere's another advantage to having multiple first-round selections: Sometimes a team doesn't need to rebuild at all.The Chiefs were coming off a 12-5 season when they traded Tyreek Hill to Miami in March 2022 for a package that included a first-round pick. They used some of that capital to move up for McDuffie at No. 21, then selected Karlaftis at No. 30. Kansas City also signed JuJu Smith-Schuster and Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who combined for 1,620 receiving yards that season, while Travis Kelce added another 1,338 yards and 12 touchdowns.(By the way, Hill picked up where he left off; in Miami, he caught 119 passes for 1,710 yards and seven touchdowns. The Dolphins finished 9-8 and reached the playoffs but lost to Buffalo in the Wild Card round with Skylar Thompson starting in place of an injured Tua Tagovailoa. Meanwhile, the Chiefs still won the Super Bowl without one of the NFL's most dynamic players.)Kansas City led the NFL in scoring in 2022, Mahomes won MVP, and the Chiefs repeated as Super Bowl champions the following season. McDuffie and Karlaftis became important pieces of the defense, but the bigger story was how Kansas City retooled both sides of the ball without missing a beat. Having Mahomes and Andy Reid certainly helped (a lot), but the Chiefs also found a way to replace Hill's production while adding young, inexpensive defensive talent.Philadelphia followed a similar path. Coming off their Super Bowl appearance, the Eagles landed Carter at No. 9 and Smith at No. 30 in 2023, then won the whole thing following the 2024 season. Carter developed into a disruptive interior defender, while Smith gave Philadelphia another young pass rusher for a defense that overwhelmed Kansas City in Super Bowl LIX.Seattle's 2023 class might be the most impressive of the group. Witherspoon, selected fifth overall, quickly became one of the league's top cornerbacks. Smith-Njigba, taken 20th, has developed into one of the NFL's most productive receivers and was named Offensive Player of the Year in 2025, the same season the Seahawks went 14-3 and won Super Bowl LX.What's different about Seattle is that it didn't have the established quarterback-coach combo that Kansas City, or even Philadelphia, enjoyed during their title runs. The Seahawks changed coaches after 2023, eventually brought in Sam Darnold and still managed to build a championship roster around young stars on both sides of the ball.Baltimore took a similar approach in 2022, drafting safety Kyle Hamilton at No. 14 and center Tyler Linderbaum at No. 25. Both developed into Pro Bowl players, and while the Ravens haven't reached the Super Bowl with that duo, they made the playoffs in three of their first four seasons. With Lamar Jackson already entrenched as an MVP-winning franchise quarterback, Baltimore could use both first-round picks to strengthen an already-talented roster.What does the historical evidence tell us?The recent success stories are equal parts impressive and fun to revisit, but they're hardly representative of what usually happens when struggling teams accumulate first-round picks.Of the 44 struggling teams (six or fewer wins) that had multiple first-round picks since 2000, 86% improved by roughly three wins or more in at least one of the next three seasons. But only 34% had two winning seasons and made the playoffs during that stretch.The numbers get even more telling: Over the next five seasons, struggling teams with multiple first-round picks won 44.9% of their games. Struggling teams with just one first-rounder? They won 45.6%. Basically, no difference.For teams that were already winning, though, the results were more encouraging. Those with multiple first-round picks won 57% of their games over the next five seasons, compared with 52.1% for teams with just one.That stability matters. Consider this: Of the 23 rebuilding teams with multiple first-round picks between 2012 and 2023, only six still had the same head coach three drafts later. Just 11 had the same GM.That's part of what makes rebuilding so difficult. Teams spend years trying to find and develop young talent, but the coaches and executives responsible for those decisions often aren't around long enough to see it through.What does the Simmons trade mean for Tennessee's rebuild?If the Titans are curious about how stockpiling picks can expedite a turnaround, they don't need to look far. They've already done it once.After going 3-13 in 2015, Tennessee traded the No. 1 overall pick to the Rams for a draft haul. The Titans used those picks to help land Jack Conklin and Derrick Henry, then went 9-7 in each of the next two seasons and won a playoff game in 2017, their first postseason victory in 14 years.A decade later, they're running it back. Tennessee just sent Simmons to Chicago for first-round picks in 2027 and 2028, plus a fourth-rounder in 2027. Heading into Week 8, the Titans have the No. 2 pick in the '27 draft, along with the 28th selection courtesy of the Bears. But here's where history offers a reality check. Of the 44 struggling teams with multiple first-round picks since 2000, 86% improved significantly within three years. Just 34% managed two winning seasons and a playoff appearance in that span. And over the next five seasons, those teams actually won at a slightly lower rate than similarly bad teams with only one first-round pick.Which brings us to Cam Ward.The Titans used the No. 1 overall pick on Ward in 2025, and while his first 24 starts have been all over the map, the team isn't ready to give up on him. Ward is 4-20 as a starter, and through those first 24 games, he ranked 51st among 56 first-round quarterbacks in EPA per dropback and 52nd in yards per attempt. The good news? Five of the six quarterbacks with similarly poor starts improved over their next 22 games. The bad news? Only two managed to get their EPA per dropback into positive territory.But given the uneven play of the 2027 quarterback class, the Titans would be better served surrounding Ward with talent rather than starting over at the position. Imagine adding Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith, undoubtedly the best player in the '27 class, to an offense that already features his former Buckeyes teammate Carnell Tate. In this particular case, "Start there and figure the rest out later" isn't a terrible strategy.It's an approach that worked for Detroit, which built around Jared Goff, and Houston, which drafted CJ Stroud and immediately surrounded him with young talent. Both became playoff contenders in short order.And that's the gamble. Simmons was already an All-Pro. Tennessee is betting the picks it got in return will help build something better. But as the Jets and Browns have learned, there's a big difference between accumulating first-round picks and turning them into a winning football team.Can the Browns, Jets and Titans turn draft capital into sustained success?If there's a franchise that knows the difference between collecting first-round picks and building a consistent winner, it's the Browns. They made five first-round selections across the 2017 and 2018 drafts, landing Myles Garrett, David Njoku, Baker Mayfield and Denzel Ward, among others. Cleveland eventually went 11-5 in 2020 and won its first playoff game since the 1994 season. But the success didn't last, and Mayfield was gone before the 2022 season.Now Cleveland gets another shot. The Browns have added promising young players in Mason Graham, Carson Schwesinger, Quinshon Judkins, Harold Fannin Jr., Spencer Fano and KC Concepcion over the last two drafts. And after trading Garrett to the Rams for Jared Verse and a haul of draft picks, GM Andrew Berry has two first-round selections in 2027 to continue the rebuild. The question remains the same one that's followed this franchise for years: Can they finally get the quarterback position right?The Jets know the feeling. Their celebrated 2022 draft produced Sauce Gardner, Garrett Wilson and Jermaine Johnson, but not a single playoff appearance. Now Gardner and Johnson are gone, New York has three more first-round picks in 2027, and the organization has another chance to turn premium selections into something more than individual success.Which brings us to Tennessee. The Titans already spent the No. 1 overall pick on Ward, and the Simmons trade gives them more opportunities to surround him with talent. Maybe that starts with Jeremiah Smith. Either way, the Titans have made their bet at QB, and the next two drafts could determine whether it pays off.And here's what stands out about the history: Most bad teams with multiple first-round picks eventually get better. But getting better and building a consistent winner are two very different things. Some find their franchise quarterback and quickly become contenders. Others draft really good players ... and somehow find themselves right back where they started a few years later.That's the challenge facing the Browns, Jets and Titans. Finding talented players isn't necessarily the problem. It's building something sustainable around them, ideally before the coaches and executives responsible for those decisions are shown the door.Because accumulating first-round picks is one thing. Turning them into a winning football team has proven to be something else entirely.

        Hello football friends, and welcome to the Thursday edition of the Pick Six newsletter! It might be time to start a newsletter where we ONLY cover big NFL trades, because this week has been crazy, and it's all thanks to the AFC South. Apparently, the bad teams in that division have decided to have a fire sale this week. The action started on Tuesday with the Colts trading both Quenton Nelson (Seahawks) and DeForest Buckner (49ers), and it continued today with the Titans sending Jeffrey Simmons to Chicago in a blockbuster deal. In a twist, Simmons' first game with the Bears will actually be coming against Nelson and the Seahawks on Monday night. We'll be covering the details of the Simmons trade in today's newsletter, plus we'll have some picks and best bets for tonight's game between the Packers and Panthers. 
As always, here's your reminder to tell all of your friends to sign up for the newsletter. To get them signed up, just click here. Let's get to the rundown.   1. Jeffrey Simmons trade: Details on the Titans-Bears deal and trade grades
                                                                    Jeff Dean/Getty Images
                                                            The Bears are officially going all-in on the 2026 season, and we know because they just mortgaged their future to land Jeffrey Simmons from the Titans in a blockbuster trade. Simmons is arguably the best defensive tackle in the NFL right now, and the Bears paid a steep price to get him. Here are the details of the deal:Bears get: Jeffrey Simmons, 2028 fifth-round pickTitans get: 2027 first-round pick and fourth-round pick, 2028 first-round pickThat's right, the Bears are sending TWO first-round picks to the Titans to make this deal happen, but that's the price you have to pay to land a player like Simmons. The 29-year-old is coming off a 2025 season where he earned first-team All-Pro honors. Since the start of last season, he has 15 sacks, which is the most in the NFL for a defensive tackle in that span. For the Bears, this fills a gaping hole on the roster. Heading into Week 8, they've only gotten one sack on the season from their interior defensive tackles, but that should change as soon as Simmons steps on the field for them. 
TRADE GRADESWhenever there's a trade, there's 100% chance we're going to hand out grades for that deal, and that's exactly what we did in this situation. Bryan DeArdo graded the deal, and here's what he came up with: Bears grade: A-. Give Chicago a ton of credit for going all-in. The Bears clearly feel they have a team capable of winning it all; they wouldn't have made a trade of this magnitude if they didn't.   By getting Simmons, the Bears have increased their odds of winning what is arguably the NFL's hardest division. Yes, it came at a monstrous cost, which is why Chicago didn't receive a perfect score for this trade. Really, the only way this trade works out for the Bears is if they win a Super Bowl. It's a massive risk, but it's one that the Bears feel is worth it. Titans grade: C+. Titans fans can rightfully sell to their fan base the value of getting two first-round picks for a non-quarterback. From a picks standpoint, the return is similar to what the Cowboys received when they traded Micah Parsons to the Packers last season. This trade sets the Titans up to draft some talented players in future drafts, but that won't matter if they draft the wrong players. Unfortunately, the Titans' track record of maximizing their draft capital hasn't been good. You can read our full story on the Simmons trade here. 


     2. Thursday night preview: Picks and best bets for Panthers at PackersWe've got an intriguing battle going on tonight in Green Bay with the Packers (4-3) facing off against the Panthers (3-3). This is a huge game for both teams. On Green Bay's end, it's already in last place in the NFC North, and it doesn't want to fall any further behind, so the Packers could really use a win here. As for the Panthers, they looked to be in control of the NFC South heading into Week 7, but then they suffered a 30-point loss to the Buccaneers on Sunday. With a loss here, they could drop out of first place by the time Week 8 is over. 
On the injury front, the Panthers won't have linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring), who is second on the team in sacks. Phillips didn't play against the Bucs on Sunday, and Carolina promptly gave up 43 points. As for the Packers, they'll be down two offensive linemen with guard/tackle Travis Glover (knee) and center Sean Rhyan (ankle) both ruled out. However, the Packers will likely have receiver Matthew Golden, who is trending toward playing despite missing two days of practice this week due to injuries to his shoulder and foot. Here's one reason why each team should be feeling confident going into the game: Why the Panthers can win: Bryce Young has been playing at an incredibly high level this year, and that might be enough for Carolina to pull off the upset. Heading into Week 8, he's averaging 285.3 passing yards per game, which is the second-highest number in the NFL. If you can throw the ball on the Packers, you can beat them. In their seven games this season, the Packers are 4-1 when they hold their opponent under 255 passing yards, but 0-2 when that number goes above 255. Not only does Young need to have a big game, but he needs to play turnover-free football. The Panthers are 0-3 this year when Young turns the ball over and 3-0 when he doesn't. Why the Packers can win: It's a good thing the Packers got Josh Jacobs back, because they're going to need him in this game. Through the first seven weeks, the Packers have had the worst rushing offense in the NFL, averaging just 59.8 yards per game. To give you an idea of how bad that is, no other team is even averaging under 70 yards per game. If the Packers are going to turn things around, this is the week to do it. Jacobs will be facing a Panthers defense that has given up the most rushing yards per game this year (153.2 yards per game). If you can run on the Panthers, you can beat them: Carolina is 1-3 this season when giving up at least 100 yards on the ground. The Packers didn't have Jacobs for their first six games, so their struggles on the ground made sense, but he's back now. This needs to be the week where the Packers finally turn to their rushing attack. You can get a full preview of the game from Jared Dubin by clicking here.If you're thinking about betting on the game, here are a couple of props. ONE RUSHING PROP I LIKE: Josh Jacobs OVER 59.5 yards (-114 at DraftKings): The Panthers have played six games this year, and SEVEN DIFFERENT players have rushed for at least 60 yards against them. Carolina can NOT stop the run, which is why I think Jacobs will coast past this number. The biggest risk with this prop is that Jacobs is playing his second game in five days after missing the first six weeks, so he could be a little sore. That being said, I have to think Matt LaFleur will do everything possible to get his ground game going in this game. ONE KICKING PROP I LIKE: Ryan Fitzgerald OVER 6.5 points (-121 at DraftKings): I'm not sure if the Packers trust their kicker right now, so I will not be touching any Trey Smack props, but I am pretty sure that the Panthers trust Fitzgerald. Through Carolina's first six games, Fitzgerald has gone 11-of-11 on field goal attempts, which makes him one of just five kickers in the NFL who're still perfect heading into Week 8. Fitzgerald has gone over 6.5 points in five of his six games this year, and I think that run will continue with an impressive performance in Green Bay.  If you're wondering how my props are doing this year, I'm 9-19 (4-10 on kicker props and 5-9 on all other props). After starting off 5-3, I'm now 4-15 on my last 19 props. It's gotten ugly. I clearly need to re-evaluate everything I'm doing in life. And yes, this is obviously a sign that you should be fading me until further notice. As a matter of fact, I might start fading myself.
And now, it's time for some picks. PICKS FOR 'TNF'Jared Dubin's pick: Packers 24-17 over PanthersJohn Breech's pick: Packers 30-23 over PanthersJordan Dajani's pick: Packers 27-23 over PanthersTyler Sullivan's pick: Packers 30-20 over PanthersPrisco's pick: Packers 31-24 over PanthersIf you want to know which way all of our experts are leaning, you can check that out on our CBSSports.com picks page.  3. NFL Week 8 picks: Undefeated Vikings go down, Steelers win AFC North showdown
                                                                    Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
                                                            Welcome to the part of the newsletter where we hand out picks. We have five NFL writers — Pete Prisco, Jordan Dajani, Tyler Sullivan, Jared Dubin and me — handing out picks each week. If you're wondering who did the best last week, it was Dubin, who went 10-4. The rest of us apparently fell asleep at the wheel with our picks because we all tied with an 8-6 record. Dubin has now finished at the top for two straight weeks. He is basically the Browns: No one believed in him at the beginning of the season, but now, he's taking down everyone. 
Anyway, if you're new here, here's how things work: I'll give you one Week 8 pick from each writer and then direct you to the rest of their picks for the week. That way, if you like their pick, you can click over and check out all their Week 8 predictions; if you hate it, you can ignore the rest and move on with your life. Pete Prisco — Lions (-3) 23-13 over Vikings. From Prisco: "The undefeated Vikings face a tough road game here against Detroit. The Lions' offense against the Minnesota defense will be a treat to watch. Jared Goff is playing at a high level right now, but Minnesota's defense is the best in the league in terms of scoring. The Vikings offense is limited, but the Detroit defense has had major problems. But they were better last week, which I think carries over. Lions take it." For the rest of Prisco's Week 8 picks, be sure to click here.Tyler Sullivan — Patriots (-7.5) 30-20 over Dolphins. From Sullivan: "While they'll be on the road, the Patriots have the rest advantage in this game after playing last Thursday. They're also simply the better team. Miami is allowing 5.7 yards per play this season and 7.8 yards per pass attempt (tied for third-highest in the NFL). Drake Maye should continue to find success through the air against a Dolphins secondary that is allowing a league-high 116.8 passer rating against. So long as they don't shoot themselves in the foot, this should be a double-digit victory for New England." For the rest of Sullivan's Week 8 picks, be sure to click here.Jordan Dajani — Broncos (+1.5) 20-16 over Chiefs. From Dajani: "Despite the one-loss record, the Chiefs again have been a bad team to bet on. They are 3-3 ATS this season and 2-9 ATS on the road since 2025. That ranks worst in the NFL entering this week. The Broncos, on the other hand, are 5-1 SU AND ATS in their last six games, which is tied with the Browns for the best ATS record in the NFL since Week 2. They have won four straight games as a home underdog." Dajani's full slate of picks will be released Friday, but you can get a preview here.Jared Dubin — Steelers (-3.5) 20-13 over Browns. From Dubin: "I don't understand how the Browns keep doing it. Every single one of their victories has required a game-winning drive in the final five minutes of the game. That's not sustainable on any level whatsoever. The Steelers don't exactly have consistency written all over them, considering the vagaries of their passing game and the fact that their three-game winning streak has come against weak opponents. But I trust Jaylen Warren and Co. more than I do the Browns at this point. " For the rest of Dubin's Week 8 picks, be sure to click here. John Breech — Bills (-3) 38-31 over Ravens. From me: "The Bills have one of the worst defenses in the NFL, and if they had any other quarterbacks, I'd probably pick against them, but they have Josh Allen. On the Ravens' end, Lamar Jackson hasn't played in a month, and although I expect him to start, I do think he'll show a small amount of rust, which means he won't be able to take full advantage of Buffalo's bad defense." For the rest of my Week 8 picks, be sure to click here. For more Week 8 NFL picks, you can check out our CBSSports.com picks page here. 
    
    

     4. Projecting all 14 teams that will make the NFL playoffs: Bills are looking superThe playoff projections are back! We first unveiled them after Week 1, and they'll be popping up in this newsletter every two weeks until the end of the season. 
Heading into Week 8, we had some big changes in our playoff projection. Last week, the Chiefs were projected to get the top seed in the AFC, and the 49ers were projected to get the top seed in the NFC. After both teams ended up losing, there's a new team at the top of each conference. If you're wondering how these projections work, we brought in our resident analytics expert, Stephen Oh. Oh simulated the rest of the season to see how things will end up playing out, and let me tell you, if his projections pan out, every folding table in Buffalo is going to get smashed. With that in mind, here's what the playoff field looks like according to Oh's projections: 
AFC1. Bills (5-1) -- AFC East champion2. Chiefs (5-1) -- AFC West champion3. Jaguars (4-2) -- AFC South champion4. Bengals (4-2) -- AFC North champion5. Broncos (5-2)6. Steelers (5-2)7. Ravens (4-3)JUST MISSED: Patriots (4-3), Browns (5-2)AFC breakdown: We have a new team being projected to win the AFC North: Cincinnati. The Bengals made history in Week 7 by becoming the first team in 75 years to win a game by at least 20 points after trailing by at least 13 points at halftime. One thing working in the Bengals' favor is their schedule. They only have to play one more road game against a team that currently has a winning record (Browns in Week 13). Speaking of the Browns, they haven't won a division title since 1989, and our computer model doesn't see that drought ending this year. Our projection has them finishing 8-9 and out of the playoffs. NFC 1. Vikings (6-0) -- NFC North champion2. 49ers (6-1) -- NFC West champion3. Falcons (3-4) -- NFC South champion4. Cowboys (3-4) -- NFC East champion5. Lions (4-2)6. Seahawks (4-3)7. Bears (5-2) JUST MISSED: Packers (4-3), Rams (3-4)
NFC breakdown: The Vikings are the only undefeated team left in the NFL and they're now being projected to finish as the top seed in the NFC. Also, the Cowboys are now projected to win the NFC East. This marks the first time all season that we've had the Cowboys projected to finish at the top of the division. Our model basically views the NFC East as a two-horse race between the Cowboys and Giants, with Dallas given a 38.5% chance to win the division and the Giants RIGHT behind them at 37.3%. One thing working in the Cowboys' favor is that they have the fourth-easiest remaining strength of schedule. Not only did the computer project the entire playoff field, but it also picked a surprising Super Bowl winner. Spoiler alert: It was the BILLS. The Bills have never won a Super Bowl, but our computer thinks that's going to change this year. If you want to know who they're playing in the big game or who they beat in the playoffs, you'll have to check out my full story here. 
 5. NFL trade deadline matchmaker: Jonathan Taylor to the NFC North? 
                                                                    Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
                                                            Don't look now, but the NFL trade deadline (Nov. 10) is right around the corner. We've already seen three big trades go down this week, with the Colts involved in two of those, and the crazy thing is they might not be done. Zach Pereles decided to play matchmaker this week, pairing trade candidates with a team that makes sense for them. And since the Colts are trading everyone, Zach made sure to include Jonathan Taylor in this exercise. Let's see where Zach has Taylor and two other trade candidates ending up: Jonathan Taylor to the Vikings. The Kyler Murray experience has been a rough one. He'll produce a big play or two with his legs or his arm, but the down-to-down consistency hasn't been close to good enough. He is 27th in sack rate, 29th in passing success rate and 31st in touchdown rate. Taylor, meanwhile, is a scoring machine, and he'd provide explosiveness to the running game, too. The Vikings saw it up close and personal Sunday, with Taylor totaling 110 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown. Aaron Jones has been playing through a knee injury, which he aggravated Sunday. The Vikings can't risk wasting their Super Bowl-caliber defense. Taylor is the solution.Saquon Barkley to the Bengals. It's been a disappointing year for Bengals running back Chase Brown. His -0.6 yards per attempt over expected is among the worst in the NFL, and it seemingly isn't clicking for him. The Bengals made a blockbuster move for Dexter Lawrence this year despite concerns about his age and productivity, and it has been hugely successful so far. Barkley could be a similar spark, especially with defenses devoting so much attention to Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.Tariq Woolen to the Lions. The Lions were in on Joey Porter Jr. before he ultimately ended up on the Cowboys. This could be another solid option for much, much cheaper. The Eagles figure to be sellers given the disastrous run of injuries on the offensive side of the ball.Zach came up with a total of nine trades, and you can check them all out here. 
    
	

     6. Extra points: Lamar Jackson might actually play this weekIt's been a busy few days around the NFL, and since it's nearly impossible to keep track of everything, I put together a quick roundup for you. Lamar Jackson tracking to play on Sunday. After missing three games with an ankle injury, Lamar Jackson is finally expected to return this week. Not only was he a full participant in practice on Wednesday, but he took all the first-team snaps, CBS Sports Insider Matt Zenitz has reported. Although Jackson practiced last week, he was limited in all three sessions, and at no point did he take the majority of the first-team snaps. Getting Jackson back would be huge news for the Ravens, who have lost two straight games and will be looking to end their skid against the Bills. Are the Vikings frauds? We wanted to know if you could win a Super Bowl with a great defense and nothing else, so Doug Clawson decided to answer that question. What he found is that if you have a historically great defense like the 2000 Ravens or 2002 Buccaneers, it's certainly possible, but it's not easy. The Vikings fit the mold of a team that could make some noise in the postseason, and if you want to see how they fit in historically with other strong defensive teams, Doug has the answer here. Why the Colts' teardown might now work. The Colts have decided to blow things up and start over. They've already made two trades this week, and there certainly could be more before the trade deadline hits. For Thursday, Ryan Wilson broke down why Indy's plan might not work in a story that's definitely worth reading here.

body:
Smith, an undefeated UFC welterweight prospect, recounts how his violent childhood and his mother's near-deadly altercation helped him get to this point
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 29, 2026

    1:10 pm ET

        A fighter's upbringing often helps explain why they pursue such hazardous work, but Jacobe Smith's early family life is particularly convincing. His childhood and family stories read like scenes from an action movie. The welterweight prospect co-headlines UFC Fight Night on Saturday against veteran Randy Brown. It's a short-notice appearance, but fighting more experienced foes on a whim is nothing new to Smith. He's been beating up older kids since before he was in middle school.Smith, a sixth-grader at the time, was outside his childhood home when an older neighbor argued with his mother. The neighbor, a high school senior, said something that Smith couldn't forgive. What happened next was probably the last thing the teenager expected."My mom was telling him to get out of our yard or something," Smith told CBS Sports. "He told her, 'Shut up, [bitch].' I don't even remember. I took off running, and there was a stump on the ground. I jumped off of it and hit him. He fell in the yard and balled up, rolling back and forth. He was a guy who beat up my cousin, who is older than me and used to bully me, and got me tough. I don't know what made me do it, but when I hit him, it changed me. I thought, 'I'm going to fight in the UFC when I'm older." 
Sign up for Paramount+ and watch UFC for no additional fee -- every UFC numbered event and UFC Fight Night is included with your subscription! Plans start as low as $8.99/month or $89.99/year!Smith remembers the punch fondly, comparing it to the brutal left hook that knocked out Preston Parsons 73 seconds into Smith's UFC debut. 
        
            
                UFC Pound-for-Pound Fighter Rankings: Alexander Volkanovski and Petr Yan shine at UFC 333
                
                    Brian Campbell                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
It's no surprise that Smith developed his mean streak at a young age, given how he talks about his parents, though he also inherited plenty of athletic ability. According to Smith, his father was drafted by the Oakland Raiders and participated in tough-man fighting competitions, reportedly earning as much as $20,000 in a single night. His mother played volleyball in the Junior Olympics.
His mother was apparently not someone to mess with. Smith told a story about an especially wild incident involving his parents outside of a nightclub, where a confrontation between his father and another man nearly turned deadly."I probably get all this 'with-it-ness' from my mother," he said. "They were at a club. My dad was getting into it with somebody. He probably wasn't even going to fight him. They're running their mouth, face-to-face, and my mom wasn't having it. She reached over him and stabbed the dude in the chest. It could have been on the side of his heart and killed him. Then a big fight broke out."Smith knows his mother's actions could have ended in tragedy. He also sees himself in her willingness to escalate a confrontation, though there's a line between the anger he feels and losing control.
"It's so crazy because I get angry, and I feel that rage, but I can't see myself losing it like that," Smith said. "When I'm in the cage, I'll do whatever it takes. If I have to get to that level, obviously, I don't have a knife, but I'm very well equipped to get you out of there, whether it's wrestling, choking you out, or knocking you out. So you guys in the welterweight division better be ready."Smith pairs natural aggression with a serious wrestling pedigree, having earned NCAA Division I All-American honors at Oklahoma State before transitioning to mixed martial arts. He's since developed the striking and submission skills to make himself dangerous anywhere. His undefeated record shows his temperament and the work he's put into becoming a complete fighter. But Smith doesn't reserve all that hostility for the Octagon. You can see shades of his parents' bold personalities in how he talks about welterweight veteran Kevin Holland. He's become a particularly sore subject for Smith. 
The two were scheduled to fight, and Smith believes Holland accepted the matchup without any real intention of following through. Their relationship has deteriorated into a personal feud, mostly conducted privately through direct messages.
"It rubs me wrong," Smith said. "When we're face-to-face, it's, 'What's up, buddy.' But as soon as a fan gets to trolling and I rock and roll with it, he has the audacity to get in my DMs and talk shit. So if we see him, we're gonna see him. I'll show him that I'm the one doing the talking."Smith insists he isn't manufacturing the animosity to start a bigger fight. He says neither fighter made their exchanges public at first. Following his most recent knockout, Smith contacted Holland directly.
"After my last knockout, I DMed him and said, 'I want you next, boy.' It went from there. He was talking mess..." Smith said. "If I see him, I'm bound to smack him in the face, outside of the cage. I don't like the dude. I'm not shying away from that. If we can't get in the cage, I'm gonna be the one doing the talking. I guarantee that."Smith doesn't ignore disrespect, whether it's in his mother's yard, in the UFC or in the training room. He and a small group of teammates recently left Fortis MMA in Dallas following behind-the-scenes disagreements with the gym's leadership. It was significant given Fortis' reputation as a respected training facility, but Smith wasn't interested in staying once the relationship soured. "I had a good training partner in Geoff Neal, plus a couple others," Smith said. "Things didn't work out with the coach, or whatever. Shit was said, and shit happened that prompted us to start our own gym. I have my own gym, and whenever I need DC, I fly out there and do part of my fight camps with him."
His path to Fortis started in California. Smith initially trained under Daniel Cormier at the American Kickboxing Academy, hoping to learn from one of MMA's most accomplished wrestlers. The financial cost eventually became too much, so he returned home."I started my career off with Daniel Cormier in California, and it was a struggle," Smith said. "I was broke then. I couldn't afford to eat some days. It was expensive out there. I moved back home to be closer to family, and Fortis was the closest thing."Cormier remains an important figure in Smith's career. A two-division UFC champion, Olympic wrestler and NCAA Division I finalist, Cormier accomplished much of what Smith aspired to as a young wrestler. Smith idolized him long before they worked together, making the opportunity to train under him worth the initial hardship.
Cormier is a wealth of knowledge on and off the mats. Asked about the most valuable advice Cormier gave him, Smith recalled a warning about fame's fleeting nature."Live in the moment and never take anything for granted," Smith said. "Most times, you get tired with all of these interviews, fans, signatures, pictures and stuff. You want to get home peacefully. He said, 'One day, people will stop running up to you, wanting autographs.' So live in the moment and don't take it for granted."Smith's rapid rise has him on the verge of the UFC welterweight rankings, and he's been more vocal about wanting a Top 15 opponent. Matchups with Holland and Brown, both former ranked fighters, suggest the promotion is moving him in that direction.
Smith graduates to the co-main event of UFC Fight Night this weekend against Brown. It's the biggest opportunity of his career, but it may not be for long. Smith hasn't received an outright guarantee that a victory will secure him a ranked opponent, but his conversations with Cormier and UFC matchmakers have him optimistic. He's even entertaining the possibility of skipping much of the rankings altogether."It's trending that way," Smith said when asked if he was given assurances that a ranked opponent was next. "Not only fans, but also talking with the matchmakers and DC. I could see, with everything that I'm piecing together, from my perspective, it'll be someone in the Top 15, or we could even see a Top 5, potentially, with the talks that I've been having."

        Victor Wembanyama's 2025-26 season -- his third in the NBA -- affirmed his status as the league's next megastar. Wembanyama led the Spurs to the 2026 NBA Finals before they lost to the Knicks in five games, and he earned the first of what figures to be many Defensive Player of the Year awards and All-NBA honors. Wembanyama has entered the 2026-27 season with sky-high expectations. The 7-foot-4 Frenchman is the favorite to win NBA MVP honors, and the Spurs are the favorites to win the 2027 championship.For the better part of his first three years in the league, Wembanyama was a beloved figure, doing things no one else could do on the court to create jaw-dropping highlights that got passed around social media and group texts. However, as the Spurs moved through the postseason, some of the love from fans started to get lost. There were moments that started to earn him a "dirty" label, including when Wembanyama clocked Naz Reid with an elbow in the second round of the playoffs against the Timberwolves. Wembanyama then irked Knicks players (and their fans) when he shoved New York star Jalen Brunson in the NBA Finals. Once viewed as a conquering hero, Wembanyama became a villain, particularly in New York. 
In a sit-down interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim that will air this Sunday night on CBS, Wembanyama was asked about that switch. He noted that he was unbothered by having a "villain" label because he was solely focused on what he was doing on the court. 60 MINUTES: Last year in the Finals you were portrayed-- as a villain. Correct me if I'm wrong, I didn't get the feeling that bothered you.VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: No, it didn't because I'm not paying attention to this-- during the Finals. I don't think any player on either team really is.While Wembanyama insists he ignored the chatter off the court, he doesn't seem to want that villain tag to last. Wembanyama added that last year's playoff run was a learning experience of toeing the line between being competitive and going to far -- which he noted he crossed on occasion. 60 MINUTES: I wondered if you didn't show, "Hey, this is part of my character too." Edgy Wemby, whatever it is. But you showed a new side of yourself.VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: It showed my limits more than anything else. Going out there, you need to play basketball. You don't need to beat the s--- out of people. [laughs] If you wanna win, at least.Wembanyama is one of the league's most openly introspective and reflective stars, even at just 23 years old. He seems to recognize that he allowed himself to get too caught up with the physicality of playoff basketball and seems determined to better understand how to play up to that line without crossing it in the manner he did at times in his first taste of the postseason. 
TUNE IN: The full interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim and Wembanyama will air Sunday, Nov. 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET, after NFL football, on CBS and stream on Paramount+. In the preseason, 60 Minutes followed Wembanyama in his native France, where he runs an annual tournament combining basketball with another one of his passions: chess.
